posts.text:
Two grain giants smashing each other's docks. A strait still shut, and Baghdad missing payroll. A president stepping ashore on islands another country claims.

Five stories from this week where the real subject was geography.

5 ways the map moved — a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ Ukraine hit major Russian grain export terminals in a Black Sea port attack — and exports from BOTH countries are now falling as each strikes the other's docks (BBC).

NYT: a Russian blockade of Ukraine's ports threatens global grain supply.

The Black Sea has one exit.

2/ Hormuz stays shut.

DW: Iraq can't export enough oil to fund its public sector — protests have started. Saudi Arabia has rerouted exports; most Gulf producers have no backup.

Riyadh can cross its own peninsula to the Red Sea. Basra can't.

3/ Settlers have besieged Palestinian families in their homes in Qusra, occupied West Bank, since Sunday — water and power cut, medical care blocked (Guardian).

BBC: forces withdrew, ~a dozen settlers remain.

Counts differ: two families (BBC/Guardian/NYT), three (Al Jazeera).

4/ Zambia voted Thursday. Hichilema's economic reforms against widespread frustration (Al Jazeera); NYT reports civil-liberties complaints against a president elected to protect them.

Landlocked, bordering eight states — the copper always leaves by someone else's coast.

5/ Japan protested Putin's visit to the disputed Kuril islands — his first, per Russian state media (BBC, single-sourced here).

Taken by Soviet forces in 1945. No Japan–Russia peace treaty since.

A head of state stepping ashore is, in territorial terms, an argument.

The data behind it — oil production, 2024.

The US, Russia and Saudi Arabia lead; Iran and Iraq a band below. Production spans three continents.

The exits don't. Much of that Gulf cluster ships through one 33 km gap.
